title: Optical instruments — microscope and telescope
notes: A compound microscope has two convex lenses. The objective has a short focal length and makes a real, enlarged image of a nearby object. The eyepiece is used as a magnifier on that image.

When the final image is at the near point D, about 25 cm, the magnification is approximately (L/f_o)(D/f_e), where L is the tube length between the two lenses. A shorter objective focal length gives a larger magnification.
An astronomical telescope looks at a distant object, so the rays arrive nearly parallel. The objective makes a real image in its focal plane. A long objective focal length gathers a large image.
For the relaxed eye the final image is at infinity, and the magnifying power is f_o / f_e. A long objective and a short eyepiece give a large power. The tube length is then about f_o + f_e.
The microscope wants a short, strong objective. The telescope wants a long objective. Swapping those choices is the usual mix-up.
A larger objective also collects more light. Magnification without light still gives a dim image, which is why telescope objectives are wide as well as long in focal length.

keyPoints: A microscope magnifies a near, tiny object.
A telescope magnifies a distant, large object.
Both use an objective and an eyepiece.
The final image is at infinity for the relaxed eye.
summary: A microscope uses a short-focus objective on a near object, and its magnification is about (L/f_o)(D/f_e). A telescope uses a long-focus objective on a distant object, and for a relaxed eye its power is f_o/f_e with tube length f_o + f_e.
